hints: Think about what type of change happens when propan-1-ol becomes an aldehyde and then a carboxylic acid, and what kind of reagent supplies oxygen for this.
walkthrough:
Recognise both changes as oxidation**
Look at $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ going to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ in reaction 2 and to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ in reaction 1. In both cases the carbon attached to oxygen gains bonds to oxygen, so both are oxidation reactions and need the same strong oxidiser.

Recall the standard AS oxidiser**
For oxidation of a primary alcohol, you use dichromate(VI) in acid. Either potassium or sodium dichromate works, but the acid ($\text{H}^{+}$, usually dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) must be present to provide the acidic conditions.
Final answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) or acidified sodium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}^{+}$ or $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}^{+}$.

hints: Compare the boiling points of an aldehyde with its alcohol and carboxylic acid, and think about what happens if the aldehyde stays in contact with hot oxidiser.
Think about which laboratory set up lets a low boiling product escape as soon as it forms, and which set up returns everything to the flask for continued reaction.
walkthrough:
See why the aldehyde is easily lost**
Propanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, has no hydrogen bonding between its own molecules like the alcohol and acid do, so it has the lowest boiling point. As soon as you warm the mixture it wants to vaporise.

Choose distillation to remove it**
If you heat with a distillation set up, the propanal vapour escapes, condenses and is collected. Because it leaves the flask, the hot acidified dichromate cannot attack it again.

Link to avoiding reaction 1**
If you used reflux instead, the condenser would return all the aldehyde to the hot oxidising mixture and it would be oxidised further to propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. So distillation stops the oxidation at the aldehyde stage.

Final answer: Carry out reaction 2 by distillation.
The aldehyde distils off as soon as it forms so it is not further oxidised to the carboxylic acid.

hints: For reaction 3, identify the change from $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ as loss of water and recall what removes water from an alcohol.
For reaction 4, identify the change from $\text{-OH}$ to $\text{-Br}$ and recall the two standard ways to supply $\text{Br}$ for this substitution.
walkthrough:
Read reaction 3 as elimination**
You are going from propan-1-ol to propene. That is loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from adjacent carbons, called dehydration. It needs a strong dehydrating acid or a hot solid catalyst.

Give the dehydration conditions**
Use concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or concentrated $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ and heat, or pass the vapour over heated $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, pumice or porcelain. The heat is essential to drive off water and form the $\text{C=C}$ bond.

Read reaction 4 as substitution**
You are swapping $\text{-OH}$ for $\text{-Br}$ to make 1-bromopropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$. Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, so you need to generate $\text{HBr}$ in situ or use a phosphorus bromide reagent.

Give the bromination conditions**
Heat with $\text{NaBr}$ or $\text{KBr}$ plus concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, which makes $\text{HBr}$ that does the substitution. Alternatively heat with red phosphorus and $\text{Br}_2$, or $\text{PBr}_3$ directly.

Final answer: reaction 3: conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or conc. $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ with heat, or $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ / pumice / porcelain / porous pot with heat.
reaction 4: $\text{KBr}$ / $\text{NaBr}$ with conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ with heat, or red P with $\text{Br}_2$ / $\text{PBr}_3$ with heat.

hints: Start by looking at the polarity of the $\text{C=O}$ bond in propanal and decide which atom the $\text{CN}^{-}$ nucleophile will attack.

Recall that a curly arrow always starts from a lone pair or a bond and points to where the electrons go, so plan the first arrow from $\text{CN}^{-}$ to carbon and the second arrow within $\text{C=O}$.
Think about what charge is left on oxygen after the $\pi$ bond breaks and what that intermediate looks like.
Consider how that negatively charged oxygen becomes $\text{-OH}$ in acid conditions and where the final curly arrow starts and ends.
walkthrough:
Set up the polar carbonyl**
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so draw $\text{C}^{\delta+}\text{=O}^{\delta-}$ in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$. That $\delta+$ carbon is the electrophile. The nucleophile is $\text{CN}^{-}$, and the reactive lone pair sits on carbon, often written as $\text{ }^{-}\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$.

Make the first attack**
Draw a curly arrow starting from the lone pair on C of $\text{CN}^{-}$ and pointing to the carbonyl carbon. At the same time draw a second curly arrow starting from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond and pointing onto O. This shows the $\pi$ electrons moving onto oxygen as the new $\text{C-C}$ bond forms.

Draw the alkoxide intermediate**
After attack you have $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}(\text{H})(\text{CN})\text{-O}^{-}$. Carbon now has four single bonds to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$, $\text{H}$, $\text{CN}$ and $\text{O}^{-}$. Put the full negative charge and the lone pairs clearly on oxygen. This is the box in the middle of the scheme.

Protonate to finish**
In the presence of $\text{H}^{+}$, draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ to $\text{H}^{+}$. This forms the $\text{O-H}$ bond and gives the cyanohydrin $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$.

Final answer: Nucleophilic addition: lone pair on C of $\text{CN}^{-}$ attacks carbonyl C with curly arrow $\text{NC}^{-}$ to $\text{C}^{\delta+}$; $\text{C=O}$ shown with $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ and curly arrow from $\text{C=O}$ bond to O; intermediate $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}(\text{CN})(\text{H})\text{O}^{-}$ with negative charge on O; lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ attacks $\text{H}^{+}$ with curly arrow $\text{O}^{-}$ to $\text{H}^{+}$ to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$.

hints: Check the four groups attached to the central carbon in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CN}$ to confirm it is a chiral centre.
Recall the conventional way to show 3D shape with solid wedge, dashed wedge and straight lines, and how a pair of enantiomers are related as mirror images.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral centre**
Look at the product carbon bonded to $\text{OH}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{CN}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$. Four different groups means it is chiral, so two non superimposable mirror images exist.

Draw the pair correctly**
Draw the central C with two bonds in the plane, for example to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CN}$. Then draw $\text{OH}$ on a solid wedge (coming out) and $\text{H}$ on a hashed wedge (going back) for one enantiomer. For the second, simply swap wedge and dash so $\text{OH}$ and $\text{H}$ exchange sides. The two drawings must be mirror images.

Final answer: Two mirror image structures of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}^{*}(\text{H})(\text{OH})(\text{CN})$ with chiral centre shown in 3D: one with $\text{OH}$ on wedge and $\text{H}$ on dash (or vice versa), the other with positions swapped, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CN}$ in plane.

hints: Picture the shape around the $\text{C=O}$ carbon in propanal and whether the $\text{CN}^{-}$ can approach from more than one direction.
Think about whether attack from above the plane versus below the plane leads to the same stereoisomer or different ones, and with what probability.
walkthrough:
See the flat starting point**
The $\text{C=O}$ carbon in propanal is trigonal planar with bond angles of about $120^{\circ}$. It is completely flat, so there is no blocking group on one face. The $\text{CN}^{-}$ ion is free to come in from above the plane or from below the plane.

Link the two attacks to the two products**
Attack from one face pushes the oxygen to the opposite side and creates one handedness at the new chiral centre. Attack from the other face creates the mirror image. Because the aldehyde itself is achiral and both approaches are identical in energy, each happens with 50:50 probability, so a racemic mixture of both enantiomers forms.

Final answer: The carbonyl group / aldehyde molecule is planar / flat / trigonal planar.
$\text{CN}^{-}$ can attack with equal chance from above or below the plane / either side, giving equal amounts of the two enantiomers.
